summary: Specifies that IPv6 hosts should retransmit Router Solicitations if no Router Advertisement arrives, with a back-off. A lost solicitation could otherwise leave a host waiting for a long time before getting network configuration.

plainLanguage.summary: If you call and nobody answers, you try again a few times, waiting longer each time, instead of giving up after one ring.

questions: why do ipv6 hosts retransmit router solicitations
how often are router solicitations retransmitted
subtitle: Hosts keep sending IPv6 Router Solicitations with exponential backoff instead of giving up after three tries.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 host sends only a few Router Solicitations when an interface starts. If they are lost, the host may have no connectivity until the next unsolicited Router Advertisement, which could be up to 30 minutes away.
tldr.mechanism: The host keeps retransmitting Router Solicitations using the exponential backoff algorithm from DHCPv6, starting at 4 seconds and capped at 3600 seconds, until it receives a Router Advertisement.
tldr.outcome: Hosts recover quickly from lost solicitations without flooding the link, at the cost of sending about one solicitation per hour forever on links that have no IPv6 router.

today: RFC 7559 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4861. It has not been obsoleted and no later RFC is recorded as updating it.

sections.title: Why Lost Solicitations Hurt
sections.content:
When an interface on an IPv6 host is initialized, RFC 4861 has the host send up to MAX_RTR_SOLICITATIONS (3) Router Solicitation (RS) messages, each separated by at least RTR_SOLICITATION_INTERVAL (4) seconds. The goal is to get a Router Advertisement quickly instead of waiting.

These solicitations can be lost. The RFC gives an example: a host is connected over Ethernet or Wi-Fi to a bridged residential gateway. Local connectivity works at interface initialization, but the upstream WAN connectivity is not active yet. The host then gives up after its initial retransmissions.
sections.plainLanguage: The host calls out for a router three times and then stops listening for answers. If the router was not ready yet, the host is stuck.

sections.title: How Long a Host Can Be Stranded
sections.content:
After the initial solicitations are lost, the host assumes there are no routers on the link, as RFC 4861 specifies. It then has no Internet connectivity until the next unsolicited multicast Router Advertisement arrives.

Those advertisements are sent at most MaxRtrAdvInterval seconds apart, with a maximum value of 1800 seconds. In the worst case, a host is therefore without connectivity for 30 minutes, which the RFC says may be unacceptable in some scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: If the router only announces itself every half hour, a host that missed the message might sit there for up to 30 minutes with nothing to do.

sections.title: The Retransmission Algorithm
sections.content:
Continuing to send at the fixed 4-second interval could create too much traffic if many hosts do it. So hosts following this specification MUST use the exponential backoff algorithm from Section 14 of RFC 3315 (DHCPv6) to keep retransmitting Router Solicitations until a Router Advertisement is received.

Hosts SHOULD use these inputs:

  • IRT (initial retransmission time): 4 seconds
  • MRT (maximum retransmission time): 3600 seconds
  • MRC (maximum retransmission count): 0
  • MRD (maximum retransmission duration): 0

The 4-second start matches the existing RTR_SOLICITATION_INTERVAL from RFC 4861, and the 3600-second cap matches the new SOL_MAX_RT value in RFC 7083. Short-term behavior therefore looks like today's networks, while long-term behavior trends toward that of DHCPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The host asks again after 4 seconds, then waits longer and longer between tries, up to an hour, so it does not annoy everyone else on the network.

sections.title: When to Stop Retransmitting
sections.content:
On links that support multicast, hosts SHOULD stop retransmitting when Router Discovery succeeds, meaning an advertisement with a non-zero Router Lifetime that results in a default route is received. If an advertisement arrives that does not result in a default route (Router Lifetime is zero), the host MUST keep retransmitting.

On non-multicast links the rule is stricter: hosts MUST continue retransmitting even after an advertisement that gives a default route. On such links an advertisement can only be triggered by a solicitation. The RFC notes that these links have special ways of sending solicitations, for example ISATAP unicasts them to specific routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Once a real router answers and says it can send your traffic out, you can stop asking. An answer that says it cannot help does not count.

sections.title: Configuration and Known Limitations
sections.content:
Implementations are encouraged to offer a configuration option to enable or disable potentially infinite retransmissions. If such an option exists, retransmissions MUST be enabled by default. Making it per-interface lets operators tune the behavior for each connected link.

There is one known limitation. When a host attaches to a network without IPv6, it previously sent 3 solicitations and stopped. With this mechanism it keeps retransmitting indefinitely at roughly 1 solicitation per hour. The RFC says it is unclear how to tell such a network apart from one where an IPv6 router is temporarily unreachable.
sections.plainLanguage: The price of never giving up is that a host on a network with no router keeps knocking about once an hour forever.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it does not present any additional security issues beyond those discussed in RFC 4861 and in the RFCs that update it.
sections.plainLanguage: This change does not open any new doors for bad guys beyond the ones that already existed.
